hook.text: The A B test is live, its users split at random between the old checkout and a new one, and the readout says the new one won. Someone wants to ship it today. Look closer first. The two groups aren't the size you asked for. It's only week one. And this was the best of ten metrics. Any one of those can turn a win into nothing.

plan.text: This round is about experiments once they're running: fourteen questions. Ten get a figure each. The other four are short enough to take in passing.

pitfalls.text: Question one. What are the common A B testing pitfalls? Five come up again and again: a split that isn't the one you set, segments that disagree with the total, a lift that fades once it isn't new, metrics read until one of them moves, and users who affect each other. Each gets a question of its own here.

srm.text: Question two. What is a sample ratio mismatch, and what causes it? You asked for fifty-fifty, and got four thousand eight hundred against five thousand two hundred.

srm-test.text: A chi-square test asks whether chance could do that. Here chi-square is sixteen, and p is about one in sixteen thousand. That's a sample ratio mismatch, an SRM. Four thousand nine hundred sixty against five thousand forty would be chance: p is point four two.

srm-cause.text: A mismatch means something treats the arms differently: bots filtered from one arm, a redirect that loses slow page loads, a logging bug. Find it before you read a single result.

nosig.text: Question three. The test shows no significant difference. What can you conclude? Only that you didn't detect one. The confidence interval says how much that's worth.

nosig-ci.text: Here are two simulated tests of a change that does nothing, on a ten percent conversion rate. Say half a point is the smallest lift worth having. With a thousand users per arm, the interval runs from minus three point two points to plus one point eight, far wider than that, so the test can't tell. With a hundred thousand per arm, it runs from minus point one to plus point four. That one does support no meaningful effect.

simpson.text: Question four. What is Simpson's paradox in an experiment? Say a new checkout rolls out unevenly: most of its users are on desktop, and most of control's are on mobile. On mobile, the new checkout converts ten percent against nine. On desktop, three and a half against three. It wins on both.

simpson-pool.text: Pool them, and it loses, four point eight against seven point eight, because desktop converts less and the new checkout got mostly desktop.

novelty.text: Question five. What are novelty and primacy effects, and how do you handle them? People click on something because it's new. That lift is real, and it doesn't last. Here one change is up fourteen percent in week one, and under one percent by week eight, while a plainer change holds at about four. Read in week one, you'd ship the wrong one.

primacy.text: Primacy runs the other way: a redesign people resist at first, until they learn it.

many.text: Question six. What is the multiple comparisons problem? Each test at a five percent level has a one in twenty chance of a false alarm. Read twenty metrics, and the chance that at least one of them fires is sixty-four percent.

many-fix.text: Here are ten simulated metrics, and three of them really moved. Five come in under point oh five, and two of those are false alarms. Bonferroni divides the five percent by ten, and keeps two: safe, but it drops a real one.

network.text: Question seven. What are network effects and interference? A standard test assumes one user's treatment can't change another user's outcome. That's SUTVA, the stable unit treatment value assumption. Give a sharing feature to half the users, and what they share reaches the other half: control gets treated too, and the difference shrinks. So randomize groups that rarely touch: clusters of friends, or whole cities.

switchback.text: Question eight. What is a switchback experiment?

concurrent.text: Question nine. How do you detect interference between experiments running at once? Compare the users who are in both with those in only one. If a pricing test's lift changes for users who also see new recommendations, the two interact. Then separate their users, run them one after the other, or analyze them together as a factorial design.

did.text: Question ten. What is a quasi-experiment, and how does difference-in-differences work? Sometimes you can't randomize: a policy starts in one city and not in another. A quasi-experiment makes use of that natural split.

did-math.text: In this simulation, the treated city's weekly sign-ups rose eight point nine after the policy. The comparison city rose two point four over the same weeks, with no policy at all. The difference of those differences, DiD for short, is six point five, close to the true effect of six. It rests on parallel trends: without the policy, the two lines would have kept moving together.

rapid-in.text: Four left. Each one is a definition and a reason.

r-ate.text: The average treatment effect, ATE, is averaged over everyone. The average treatment effect on the treated, ATT, only over those who actually got it. A randomized test makes them match. Observational data can pull them apart.

r-long.text: Long-running experiments drift: seasons turn, and other launches land on the same users. Freeze the scope, run at least one full business cycle, and set the end date in advance.

r-holdback.text: A holdback keeps a few percent of users on the old version after launch, to check months later that the win lasted.

r-meta.text: And a meta-analysis pools many experiments. Rather than averaging their headlines, it weights each by its precision, so big, tight experiments count more.

next.text: Every answer here assumed someone had already chosen what to test and what to count. Making that choice is the product-sense round. Next: product sense and metrics.

simpson-def.text: That's Simpson's paradox: a result that holds in every segment flips in the total, because the arms have a different mix. In a randomized test the mix should match, so check it in each arm: a gap is a bug, like an SRM, and the fair comparison is the one within each segment.

primacy-fix.text: For both, run past the first weeks, and compare new users, who never saw the old version, with returning ones.

many-bh.text: Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate, the expected share of your hits that are false. It gives the smallest p-value a bar of one tenth of five percent, the next two tenths, and so on, and keeps everything up to the last one under its bar: here, the three real ones.

many-end.text: Better still, name one primary metric before the test starts.

sb-pool.text: In a marketplace, riders and drivers share one pool, so you can't split users: a treated rider who books faster takes a driver from a control rider, and the split overstates the effect.

sb-time.text: Split time instead: the whole city gets the new version for an hour, then the old one, switching at random.

sb-carry.text: One hour spills into the next, so drop the first minutes of each hour as a washout, and count hours, not users, as the sample.

r-curse.text: Watch for the winner's curse: at twenty percent power, the results that reached significance overstate the true effect more than twofold.

did-check.text: You can't see that after the policy, but you can check the weeks before it: here the two cities rose together.
